title: TLS in 2026: short-lived certificates without the pager
speaker: Ingrid Solberg, Platform Security, Fjordline
abstract: Public CAs are moving to 90-day certificates and internal PKI teams are already issuing for seven days or less. Ingrid walks through how Fjordline automated issuance and rotation with ACME and cert-manager across a few hundred services, kept mTLS between them boring, and built dashboards that show a certificate ageing long before it expires. Expect concrete failure stories: the renewal hook that silently stopped, the load balancer that cached an old chain, and the on-call rota that no longer has 'expired cert' as an incident category. Aimed at platform and security engineers who still treat expiry as a date on a calendar.

title: Kubernetes at the edge of sanity: multi-tenant clusters with GitOps
speaker: Mateusz Kowalczyk, SRE Lead, Lumen Grid
abstract: One cluster, twelve teams, and a promise that none of them will ever notice each other. Mateusz shows the layering that makes that promise hold: dedicated node pools and taints for the noisy workloads, network policy that denies by default, admission control that rejects the manifest before it reaches the scheduler, and per-tenant quotas that are generated rather than hand-edited. The second half is the Flux repository layout that survived the third team joining, the first external partner, and the audit that asked for proof of isolation. Bring your own GitOps horror story; there is time for them at the end.

title: AI agents in production: identity, guardrails and who pays when they go wrong
speaker: Yara Haddad, Head of Applied AI, Northbeam
abstract: Northbeam runs agents that touch customer accounts, and this is the talk about everything that had to exist before that was allowed. Yara covers giving each agent a workload identity instead of a shared API key, scoping the tools it may call through MCP servers with explicit allow-lists, and the evaluation gate an agent must pass before it sees real data. The uncomfortable part is organisational: who reviews an agent's actions, what the audit log must contain, and who pays when a tool call moves money the wrong way. Useful for anyone shipping LLM agents, and for the security and compliance people who have to sign them off.

title: Microsoft Exchange hybrid: the last mile to the cloud
speaker: Derek Oyelaran, Messaging Architect, Halcyon Health
abstract: Halcyon Health kept two on-premises Exchange servers alive for six years after moving mailboxes to Exchange Online, because nobody could say what still depended on them. Derek explains how the team mapped hybrid identity through Entra, found the printers and clinical systems still relaying mail through the old servers, preserved compliance holds and retention across the move, and planned the cut-over weekend so that Monday morning was uneventful. He ends with the three mistakes that cost them a weekend each, so you can skip them. For Microsoft 365 administrators, identity engineers and anyone in a regulated organisation with a server they are afraid to switch off.

title: Azure VMs without the surprise bill: sizing, reservations and spot
speaker: Priyanka Rao, Cloud FinOps, Meridian Retail
abstract: Meridian Retail cut its Azure virtual machine spend by a third without moving a single workload, and Priyanka shows the spreadsheet-free way they did it. She covers choosing VM families by what the workload actually does, when reservations and savings plans pay off and when they lock you into last year's architecture, running batch jobs on spot capacity with checkpointing so evictions are an inconvenience rather than an outage, and the tagging discipline that lets finance read the bill without calling engineering. Practical for cloud engineers, platform teams and anyone who has been asked why the invoice went up.

title: AWS Bedrock in anger: model choice, guardrails and RAG that holds up
speaker: Tomás Lindgren, Principal Engineer, Verdant Logistics
abstract: Verdant Logistics answers questions over shipping contracts and customs paperwork with retrieval on Bedrock, and the first version confidently invented a tariff. Tomás walks through how they chose between the hosted models, built a retrieval pipeline over PDFs full of tables that stops hallucinating the quarterly numbers, used Bedrock Guardrails to keep answers inside the documents, and measured all of it with an evaluation set the operations team maintains. He closes with real cost figures at production traffic and the trade-offs between vector search, hybrid search and simply reading the whole document. For engineers building retrieval-augmented products on AWS and the people who review their bills.
